p.src: That night the two armies fought in confusion until daybreak, when each side withdrew its troops. Ma Chao encamped at the mouth of the Wei River and divided his forces day and night to attack from front and rear. On the Wei River, Cao Cao chained boats and rafts together to make three floating bridges connecting with the southern bank. Cao Ren led troops to establish camps on both sides of the river and linked the supply wagons together as a barrier. When Ma Chao heard of this, he ordered every soldier to carry a bundle of grass and bring fire, then joined Han Sui in a concerted assault on the camp; they piled up the grass and set it fiercely ablaze. Cao Cao's troops could not withstand them and abandoned the camp in flight. The wagons and floating bridges were all burned and destroyed. The Xiliang army won a great victory and cut off the Wei River crossing. Unable to establish a camp, Cao Cao grew anxious and fearful. Xun You said, “We can take sand and earth from the Wei River and build an earthen fortress that will be strong enough to defend.” Cao Cao assigned thirty thousand soldiers to carry earth and build the fortress. Ma Chao then sent Pang De and Ma Dai, each with five hundred cavalrymen, to charge back and forth against them; moreover, the sandy soil would not hold, and each section collapsed as soon as it was raised, leaving Cao Cao at a loss.

p.src: It was the end of the ninth month. The weather suddenly turned cold, and dense crimson clouds covered the sky without clearing for days. Cao Cao sat troubled in his camp. Suddenly someone reported, “An old man has come to see the Chancellor and wishes to present a strategy.” Cao Cao invited him in. The man had the spare frame of a crane and the bearing of a pine, with an ancient and venerable appearance. On being questioned, he proved to be a man of Jingzhao who lived in seclusion on Mount Zhongnan; his surname was Lou, his courtesy name Zibo, and his Daoist sobriquet the Recluse Dreaming of Plum Blossoms. Cao Cao received him with the courtesies due a guest. Zibo said, “My lord Chancellor has long wished to cross the Wei and establish a camp. Why do you not seize this opportunity to build it?” Cao Cao said, “On sandy ground the ramparts cannot be built. What sound plan can you, sir, teach me?” Zibo replied, “My lord Chancellor commands troops with divine skill; can you truly be unaware of the season and weather? Clouds have gathered for days; once the north wind rises, there is certain to be a hard freeze. After the wind begins, have the soldiers carry earth and pour water over it; by daybreak the earthen fortress will be complete.”

p.src: Cao Cao suddenly understood and rewarded Zibo handsomely. Zibo declined the reward and departed. That night a mighty north wind arose. Cao Cao drove all his soldiers to carry earth and pour water upon it. As they had no vessels for holding water, they made silk bags, filled them with water, and drenched the earth, which froze as fast as they built. By daybreak the sand and earth had frozen solid, and the earthen fortress was complete. A spy reported the news to Ma Chao. Ma Chao led troops to inspect it and was greatly astonished, suspecting divine aid. The next day he assembled his great army and advanced to the beat of drums. Cao Cao rode out of camp himself, with only Xu Chu following behind. Cao Cao raised his whip and shouted, “Mengde has come here alone on horseback. Let Ma Chao come out and speak with me!” Ma Chao rode out with his spear leveled. Cao Cao said, “You mocked me for being unable to establish my camp, but now Heaven has built it for me in a single night. Why do you not surrender at once?”

p.src: Ma Chao flew into a rage and meant to dash forward and seize him, but behind Cao Cao he saw a man with fierce, round, glaring eyes, holding a steel saber and sitting motionless on his reined-in horse. Suspecting that the man was Xu Chu, Ma Chao raised his whip and asked, “I hear there is a Tiger Marquis in your army. Where is he?” Xu Chu raised his saber and roared, “I am Xu Chu of Qiao Commandery!” His eyes flashed with an uncanny light, and his bearing was majestic and fearsome. Ma Chao dared not make a move and reined his horse around. Cao Cao likewise led Xu Chu back to camp. The soldiers of both armies watched in amazement. Cao Cao said to his generals, “Even the rebels know that Zhongkang is the Tiger Marquis?” From then on, everyone in the army called Xu Chu the Tiger Marquis. Xu Chu said, “Tomorrow I shall capture Ma Chao without fail.” Cao Cao said, “Ma Chao is valiant. You must not underestimate him.” Xu Chu replied, “I swear to fight him to the death!” He at once sent a challenge declaring that the Tiger Marquis alone challenged Ma Chao to a decisive battle the following day. On receiving the letter, Ma Chao angrily exclaimed, “How dare he insult me so!” He immediately wrote in reply that on the following day he swore to slay the Tiger Madman.

p.src: The next day both armies left their camps and drew up in battle formation. Ma Chao assigned Pang De to the left wing, Ma Dai to the right, and Han Sui to command the center. Ma Chao galloped forward with leveled spear, halted before the formation, and shouted, “Tiger Madman, come out at once!” Beneath the commander's standard, Cao Cao looked back at his generals and said, “Ma Chao's valor is no less than Lü Bu's.” Before he had finished speaking, Xu Chu spurred his horse and rode out brandishing his saber. Ma Chao leveled his spear and engaged him. They fought for more than a hundred bouts without either gaining the upper hand. When their horses tired, each returned to his army, changed mounts, and came out before the lines again. They fought another hundred and more bouts, still without a victor. Xu Chu's battle fury rose. He raced back to his lines, stripped off his armor, and, with every sinew bulging on his bare body, took up his saber, vaulted onto his horse, and returned to fight Ma Chao to the death. Both armies were appalled. The two fought for more than thirty further bouts. Xu Chu mustered his might, raised his saber, and slashed at Ma Chao. Ma Chao dodged the blow and thrust his spear straight at Xu Chu's heart. Xu Chu cast aside his saber and trapped the spear beneath his arm. The two struggled for possession of the spear on horseback. Xu Chu's strength was immense; with a sharp crack he snapped the spear shaft, and each man seized one half and struck wildly at the other from horseback. Fearing harm might befall Xu Chu, Cao Cao ordered the two generals Xiahou Yuan and Cao Hong to ride out together and attack Ma Chao from both sides. Seeing Cao Cao's generals ride out together, Pang De and Ma Dai signaled the armored cavalry on both wings, which charged headlong through the enemy and plunged into the melee. Cao Cao's troops fell into great disorder. Xu Chu was struck by two arrows in the arm. The generals hastily retreated into the camp. Ma Chao pursued them to the riverbank, and more than half of Cao Cao's troops were killed or wounded. Cao Cao ordered the gates firmly shut and forbade anyone to go out. Ma Chao returned to the mouth of the Wei and said to Han Sui, “Of all the fierce fighters I have seen, none equals Xu Chu. He truly is the Tiger Madman!”

p.src: Now Cao Cao judged that Ma Chao could be defeated by stratagem, so he secretly ordered Xu Huang and Zhu Ling to cross the river with all their troops and establish a camp to the west, preparing to attack from front and rear. One day, from atop the fortress, Cao Cao saw Ma Chao lead several hundred horsemen straight up to the camp, racing back and forth like the wind. Cao Cao watched for a long while, then flung his helmet to the ground and said, “If that Ma boy does not die, I shall have no place to be buried!” Hearing this, Xiahou Yuan was filled with indignation and declared sternly, “I would sooner die on this ground than fail to destroy that rebel Ma!” He then led more than a thousand of his own troops, threw open the camp gates, and charged straight after Ma Chao. Cao Cao urgently tried but failed to stop him. Fearing disaster, he hastily mounted his own horse and rode forward to support him. When Ma Chao saw Cao Cao's troops approaching, he turned his vanguard into the rear guard and his rear guard into the vanguard, then deployed them in a single line. When Xiahou Yuan arrived, Ma Chao met him in combat. Amid the turmoil Ma Chao sighted Cao Cao in the distance, broke off from Xiahou Yuan, and charged straight at Cao Cao. Cao Cao was greatly alarmed, wheeled his horse around, and fled. Cao Cao's troops fell into utter confusion.

p.src: As the pursuit continued, a sudden report came that one of Cao Cao’s armies had already crossed west of the river and made camp. Ma Chao was greatly alarmed. Abandoning the pursuit, he hastily recalled his troops to camp and consulted Han Sui, saying, “Cao Cao’s forces have taken advantage of our exposed position and crossed west of the river. We shall now be attacked from front and rear. What are we to do?” His officer Li Kan said, “It would be best to cede territory and sue for peace, so that both sides may suspend hostilities for the time being. Once we have weathered the winter and spring brings warmer days, we can devise another plan.” Han Sui said, “Li Kan’s proposal is excellent. We should follow it.” Ma Chao hesitated and could not decide. Yang Qiu and Hou Xuan both urged him to seek peace. Han Sui therefore sent Yang Qiu as his envoy directly to Cao Cao’s camp with a letter proposing to cede territory in exchange for peace. Cao Cao said, “Return to your camp for now. Tomorrow I shall send someone with my reply.” Yang Qiu took his leave. Jia Xu entered and asked Cao Cao, “What does the Chancellor intend to do?” Cao Cao said, “What is your opinion?” Jia Xu replied, “In war, there can never be too much deception. Pretend to accept their offer, then employ a scheme of dissension to make Han Sui and Ma Chao distrust each other. They can then be routed at a single stroke.” Cao Cao clapped his hands in delight and said, “The finest minds in the realm often arrive at the same conclusion. Wenhe’s plan is precisely what I had in mind.” He therefore sent back a letter saying, “Wait while I gradually withdraw my troops; then I shall return your lands west of the river.” At the same time, he ordered a floating bridge constructed, as though preparing to withdraw. When Ma Chao received the letter, he said to Han Sui, “Although Cao Cao has agreed to peace, that treacherous hero is impossible to fathom. If we fail to prepare, we may instead fall under his control. You and I, Uncle, shall take turns deploying our forces. Today you will face Cao Cao while I face Xu Huang; tomorrow I shall face Cao Cao while you face Xu Huang. Thus we shall guard both fronts against any deception.”

p.src: Han Sui followed this plan, and before long someone reported it to Cao Cao. Cao Cao turned to Jia Xu and said, “My plan has succeeded!” He asked, “Who is due to face me tomorrow?” The informant replied, “Han Sui.” The next day, Cao Cao led his generals out of camp, surrounded on either side by his men. Cao Cao alone rode conspicuously in the center. Many of Han Sui’s soldiers had never seen him before and came out of their ranks to look. Cao Cao called out loudly, “Do you soldiers wish to see Lord Cao? I am a man like any other. I do not have four eyes and two mouths—only rather more cunning.”

p.src: The soldiers all showed fear on their faces. Cao Cao sent a man across the lines to tell Han Sui, “The Chancellor respectfully invites General Han to confer with him.” Han Sui immediately rode out from his lines. Seeing that Cao Cao wore neither armor nor weapons, he too cast off his armor and rode out alone in light attire. Their horses met head to head, and each held his reins as they spoke. Cao Cao said, “Your father and I were recommended as Filial and Incorrupt candidates at the same time, and I always treated him as an uncle. You and I also entered official life together, and many years have passed before we knew it. How old might you be this year, General?” Han Sui replied, “I am forty.” Cao Cao said, “When we were in the capital long ago, we were both in the bloom of youth. Who would have thought we should now be middle-aged! How I wish we might enjoy peace together throughout the realm!” He spoke at length only of old times, never once mentioning military affairs, and laughed heartily when he had finished. They conversed for two hours before turning their horses apart, each returning to his own camp.

p.src: Now Cao Cao, upon returning to camp, said to Jia Xu, “Did you understand the purpose of my conversation before the lines?” Jia Xu replied, “The idea was ingenious, but it is not yet enough to divide the two men. I have a plan that will make Han Sui and Ma Chao turn upon and kill each other.” Cao Cao asked him to explain the plan. Jia Xu said, “Ma Chao is merely a valiant warrior and understands nothing of subtle schemes. My lord Chancellor should write a letter in his own hand addressed solely to Han Sui, making some passages deliberately vague and personally crossing out and altering the crucial parts. Then seal it and send it to Han Sui, while intentionally ensuring that Ma Chao learns of it. Ma Chao will certainly demand to see the letter. When he sees that every important passage has been altered or blotted out, he will assume that Han Sui himself made the alterations for fear that Ma Chao might learn some vital secret. This will confirm his suspicions about their private meeting on horseback. Once suspicion arises, disorder is sure to follow. I shall also secretly win over the generals under Han Sui and make them sow discord among one another. Then Ma Chao can be dealt with.” Cao Cao said, “A splendid plan.” He immediately wrote a letter, altering and blotting out all its crucial passages. He then sealed it securely and deliberately sent a large escort to deliver it to the other camp; once they had handed over the letter, they returned.

p.src: Sure enough, someone reported it to Ma Chao. His suspicions deepened, and he went straight to Han Sui to demand the letter. Han Sui handed it to him. Seeing the altered and blotted-out words, Ma Chao asked Han Sui, “Why is everything in this letter changed and obscured?” Han Sui replied, “The letter came this way. I do not know why.” Ma Chao said, “Who would send someone a rough draft? You must have blotted out the passages yourself, Uncle, for fear I might learn the details.” Han Sui said, “Perhaps Cao Cao mistakenly sealed and sent the rough draft.” Ma Chao said, “I do not believe that either. Cao Cao is a meticulous man. How could he make such a mistake? You and I have joined forces to destroy the traitor. Why have you suddenly conceived a different intent?” Han Sui replied, “If you do not trust my loyalty, tomorrow I shall lure Cao Cao into conversation before the lines. You can charge out from within our ranks and kill him with a single thrust of your spear.” Ma Chao said, “Only then will your true loyalty be proved, Uncle.” The two men made their agreement.

p.src: The next day, Han Sui led five generals—Hou Xuan, Li Kan, Liang Xing, Ma Wan, and Yang Qiu—out before the lines. Ma Chao concealed himself in the shadow of the gate. Han Sui sent a man to the front of Cao Cao’s camp to call loudly, “General Han invites the Chancellor to come and talk.” Cao Cao ordered Cao Hong to lead several dozen horsemen straight out before the lines to meet Han Sui. When their horses were several paces apart, Cao Hong leaned forward in his saddle and said, “Do not fail in what the Chancellor privately charged you with last night, General.” As soon as he had spoken, he turned his horse back. Hearing this, Ma Chao flew into a rage, leveled his spear, spurred his horse forward, and made to stab Han Sui. The five generals stopped him, soothed the quarrel, and brought them back to camp. Han Sui said, “Worthy nephew, cease your suspicions. I harbor no evil intent.” But Ma Chao refused to believe him and departed in bitter resentment. Han Sui consulted the five generals, saying, “How can this affair be explained?” Yang Qiu said, “Ma Chao relies on his martial prowess and has always had a mind to domineer over you, my lord. Even if he defeats Cao Cao, how could he be willing to share power with you? In my humble opinion, we should secretly go over to Lord Cao. In time, you will not fail to receive the rank of marquis.” Han Sui said, “Ma Teng and I once swore brotherhood. How could I bear to betray him?” Yang Qiu said, “Matters have come to this. There is no other choice.” Han Sui asked, “Who can carry the message?” Yang Qiu replied, “I am willing to go.” Han Sui then wrote a secret letter and sent Yang Qiu to Cao Cao’s camp to discuss their surrender.

p.src: Cao Cao was delighted. He promised to enfeoff Han Sui as Marquis of Xiliang and appoint Yang Qiu as Administrator of Xiliang, while granting official rank and titles to all the others. They agreed to use a fire as their signal and join forces against Ma Chao. Yang Qiu bowed and took his leave. Returning to Han Sui, he related everything in detail: “We have agreed to set a fire tonight and attack from within and without.” Han Sui was overjoyed. He ordered his soldiers to pile dry firewood behind the central command tent, while each of the five generals armed himself with sword and saber and stood ready. Han Sui considered arranging a banquet to lure Ma Chao there and kill him at the feast, but he still hesitated and had not decided.

p.src: But Ma Chao had already learned every detail. Taking several attendants with him, he went ahead sword in hand and ordered Pang De and Ma Dai to support him from the rear. Ma Chao slipped into Han Sui's tent and saw the five commanders speaking secretly with him. He heard Yang Qiu say, “There must be no delay. Let us act at once!” Enraged, Ma Chao burst in brandishing his sword and shouted, “How dare you villains plot to murder me!” They were all greatly alarmed. Ma Chao slashed his sword straight at Han Sui's face. Han Sui desperately raised a hand to ward it off, and his left hand was severed at once. The five commanders drew their blades and rushed at him together. Ma Chao bounded outside the tent, where the five commanders surrounded him and fought in a confused melee. Alone, Ma Chao wielded his treasured sword and held all five at bay. Where the sword flashed, fresh blood sprayed: Ma Wan was hewn down, Liang Xing was slain, and the remaining three fled for their lives. When Ma Chao reentered the tent to kill Han Sui, the attendants had already carried him away. A fire broke out behind the tent, and the troops in every camp stirred. Ma Chao hastily mounted his horse. Pang De and Ma Dai also arrived, and a chaotic battle ensued. As Ma Chao led his troops in an attempt to break out, Cao Cao's forces closed in from every side: Xu Chu barred the front, Xu Huang the rear, Xiahou Yuan the left, and Cao Hong the right, while the soldiers of Xiliang slaughtered one another. Unable to find Pang De or Ma Dai, Ma Chao led a little over a hundred horsemen to block the Wei Bridge.

p.src: At first light, he saw Li Kan leading a force beneath the bridge. Ma Chao leveled his spear, spurred his horse, and gave chase. Li Kan fled, trailing his spear behind him. Just then Yu Jin came up behind Ma Chao. He drew his bow and shot, but Ma Chao heard the bowstring twang behind him and swiftly dodged. The arrow struck Li Kan ahead instead, knocking him from his horse and killing him. Ma Chao wheeled his horse and charged at Yu Jin. Yu Jin spurred his horse and escaped. Ma Chao returned to the bridge and took up his position. Cao Cao's troops arrived in great numbers from front and rear; the Tiger Guard led the assault, loosing volleys of arrows at Ma Chao from both sides. Ma Chao swept them aside with his spear, and the arrows showered to the ground. Ma Chao ordered his riders to charge back and forth, but Cao Cao's encirclement was so dense and firm that they could not break through. With a mighty shout upon the bridge, Ma Chao fought his way to the north bank, but all his riders were cut off behind him. Ma Chao charged alone through the enemy ranks, until a hidden crossbow bolt brought down his mount. Ma Chao fell to the ground, and Cao Cao's soldiers closed in.

p.src: At that perilous moment, a body of troops suddenly charged in from the northwest. It was Pang De and Ma Dai. The two men rescued Ma Chao. They gave Ma Chao a warhorse from among their troops. Mounting, he fought open a bloody path, and they fled northwest. When Cao Cao heard that Ma Chao had escaped, he ordered his commanders, “Whether day or night, you must pursue and catch that Ma fellow. Whoever brings me his head shall receive a thousand gold pieces and be enfeoffed as a marquis of ten thousand households. Whoever captures him alive shall be appointed commander-in-chief.” The commanders received the order. Each eager to claim the merit, they streamed after him in pursuit. Ma Chao paid no heed to the exhaustion of men and horses and thought only of fleeing. His mounted followers gradually scattered. Many foot soldiers who could not keep up were captured. Only a little over thirty horsemen remained as he and Pang De and Ma Dai made for Longxi and Lintao.

p.src: Cao Cao personally pursued as far as Anding. Learning that Ma Chao was already far away, he finally recalled his troops and returned to Chang'an. All the commanders assembled. Han Sui, having lost his left hand, was now disabled. Cao Cao ordered him to rest his horses at Chang'an and conferred upon him the title Marquis of Xiliang. Yang Qiu and Hou Xuan were both enfeoffed as marquises and ordered to guard the mouth of the Wei. Cao Cao then ordered the army to return to the capital, Xudu. Yang Fu, courtesy name Yishan, an army adviser of Liangzhou, came straight to Chang'an to see Cao Cao. Cao Cao asked what he wanted. Yang Fu said, “Ma Chao possesses the valor of Lü Bu and has won the deep allegiance of the Qiang people. If Your Excellency does not seize this momentum and eradicate him, then once he has rebuilt his strength, the commanderies west of Longshan will no longer belong to the state. I beg Your Excellency not to withdraw the army yet.” Cao Cao replied, “I had intended to leave troops behind to campaign against him, but the Central Plain is beset with troubles and the south remains unsettled, so I cannot stay here long. You must safeguard the region for me.”

p.src: Yang Fu accepted the charge and further recommended Wei Kang as Inspector of Liangzhou. Together they were to command troops stationed at Jicheng as a defense against Ma Chao. Before departing, Yang Fu petitioned Cao Cao, “A powerful force must be left at Chang'an to provide support from the rear.” Cao Cao said, “I have already arranged it. Set your mind at ease.” Yang Fu took his leave and departed. The commanders all asked, “When the rebels first occupied Tong Pass and the road north of the Wei lay open, why did Your Excellency not attack Fengyi from Hedong, but instead hold at Tong Pass, delay there many days, and only afterward cross northward and establish a fortified camp?” Cao Cao replied, “When the rebels first held Tong Pass, had I gone directly to Hedong upon arriving, they would certainly have divided the forces of their various camps among the crossings, and then it would have been impossible to cross west of the Yellow River. I therefore massed a great army before Tong Pass, causing all the rebels to defend the south and leave the west bank unprepared. Thus Xu Huang and Zhu Ling were able to cross. Only then did I lead the army across to the north, chaining carts and planting palisades to form a walled passage, and building a city of ice. I wanted the rebels to believe me weak, grow arrogant, and neglect their defenses. Then I deftly employed a scheme of dissension while conserving the soldiers' strength, and destroyed the enemy in a single stroke. This is precisely what is meant by ‘the swift thunderclap leaves no time to cover one's ears.’ The transformations of warfare are certainly not confined to a single method.”

p.src: The commanders asked again, “Whenever Your Excellency heard that the rebels were adding troops and swelling their numbers, you looked pleased. Why was that?” Cao Cao replied, “The Guanzhong region is remote. Had the various rebels each relied upon their own rugged strongholds, they could not have been pacified without a campaign of one or two years. Now they had all gathered in one place. Though numerous, they were not united in purpose and could easily be divided. They could be wiped out in a single stroke; that was why I rejoiced.” The commanders bowed and said, “Your Excellency's divine strategy is beyond us all!” Cao Cao said, “I also relied upon the efforts of all you civil and military officers.” He then richly rewarded the armies and left Xiahou Yuan with troops stationed at Chang'an. The surrendered troops were divided among the various units. Xiahou Yuan recommended Zhang Ji, courtesy name Derong, a native of Gaoling in Fengyi, to be Administrator of Jingzhao and guard Chang'an together with him. Cao Cao withdrew his army and returned to the capital. Emperor Xian had the imperial carriage prepared and went beyond the city walls to welcome him. An edict granted Cao Cao the privileges of receiving homage without having his name announced, entering court without hurrying, and ascending the hall armed with sword and shod in his boots, following the precedent of Xiao He, chancellor of Han. From that time onward, his might awed both the court and the realm beyond.

p.src: When this news reached Hanzhong, it soon alarmed Zhang Lu, Administrator of Hanning. Zhang Lu was a native of Feng in the state of Pei. His grandfather Zhang Ling had composed Daoist writings on Mount Huming in western Sichuan to delude the people, and all revered him. After Zhang Ling died, his son Zhang Heng continued the practice. Any commoner who came to study the Way contributed five pecks of rice, and so they were commonly called the “Rice Rebels.” When Zhang Heng died, Zhang Lu continued it. In Hanzhong, Zhang Lu styled himself the “Master and Lord.” Those who came to study the Way were all called “Ghost Soldiers.” Their leaders were called “Libationers.” Those commanding many followers were called “Senior Libationers of a Parish.” They made sincerity and good faith their chief principles and permitted no deceit. Whenever anyone fell ill, an altar was erected and the sick person was placed alone in a quiet chamber to reflect upon his transgressions and confess them openly; only then were prayers offered on his behalf. Those who presided over the prayers were called “Libationers Supervising the Ordinances.” The rite of prayer consisted of writing down the patient's name, declaring his intent to submit and confess his guilt, and composing three copies of a document called the “Handwritten Petitions to the Three Officials.” One copy was burned on a mountaintop as a memorial to Heaven, one was buried in the earth as a memorial to Earth, and one was sunk beneath the water as an appeal to the Official of Water. Afterward, if the illness was cured, five pecks of rice were given in thanks. They also built charitable lodgings fully stocked with rice, firewood, and meat, allowing travelers to take and eat as much as they needed. Those who took too much would incur Heaven's punishment. Anyone within the territory who broke the law was invariably pardoned three times. Only if the offender failed to reform was punishment imposed. There were no government officials anywhere; everything was administered by the Libationers. In this manner Zhang Lu had held Hanzhong as a powerful domain for thirty years. The imperial government, considering the region too distant to conquer, simply appointed Zhang Lu General of the Household Who Guards the South and Administrator of Hanning, requiring of him only the regular delivery of tribute.
